articles.topic: One avocado daily cuts heart risk
articles.headline: One Avocado a Day Just Cut Your Heart Disease Risk. Here's How.
articles.body: Researchers at Penn State tracked 786 adults with obesity for six months. Those who added one avocado daily—without changing anything else—reduced their harmful LDL cholesterol particles by an amount that drops heart disease risk by about 4%. The effect wasn't about weight loss. It was pure nutrition: avocados pack monounsaturated fats, fiber, and plant compounds that actively improve how your body handles cholesterol. One small, consistent change. Real results.
articles.takeaway: Add one avocado to your daily routine if you have abdominal obesity. It's a practical, zero-friction way to shift your heart health baseline.
articles.source: Penn State University / Journal of Clinical Lipidology

articles.topic: Daily fiber heals knee arthritis pain
articles.headline: Your Gut Just Became Your Joint's Best Friend.
articles.body: A simple prebiotic fiber supplement just did something exercise programs struggle to do: cut knee arthritis pain in six weeks without the dropout rate. In the INSPIRE trial, 117 adults took inulin daily while others did digital physiotherapy. The fiber group won on pain reduction, grip strength, and staying committed. Why? Gut bacteria process the fiber and produce butyrate, a compound that kills inflammation where it counts. It's a gut-muscle-pain axis researchers didn't fully understand until now.
articles.takeaway: If knee arthritis limits you, try a daily inulin supplement. It's easier to stick with than exercise programs and the science now backs it.

articles.topic: Wearable patch spots heart rhythms with precision
articles.headline: A Patch the Size of a Postage Stamp Just Nailed Heart Arrhythmias.
articles.body: <cite index="71-1">A flexible computing patch developed at the University of Chicago now detects life-threatening heart arrhythmias with 99.6% accuracy, processing all data on the body itself rather than offloading to a cloud.</cite> This changes everything about wearable health monitoring. No cloud dependency. No latency. No waiting. The patch does all the heavy lifting while sitting on your chest. For people at risk of sudden cardiac events, this is the difference between catching something early and missing it.
articles.takeaway: Next-gen cardiac patches are here. If your doctor suggests monitoring for arrhythmias, ask about on-device AI patches—they're becoming standard care.

articles.headline: Your Morning Coffee Just Bought You Liver Insurance.
articles.body: <cite index="1-1,1-3">A major long-term study linked coffee consumption with lower risks of cirrhosis, liver cancer, and death from liver disease. Coffee drinkers also showed healthier liver scans and blood protein patterns, with less fat, inflammation, and scarring.</cite> This isn't about the caffeine. It's the polyphenols—plant compounds in coffee that activate protective proteins in your body. The effect is dose-responsive: more coffee, more protection. If liver disease runs in your family or you've had alcohol history, this might be the simplest intervention your doctor suggests.
articles.takeaway: Regular coffee consumption protects your liver at scale. Three to five cups daily is where the research shows the strongest benefit.

workout.title: Reset and Release: Full-Body Tension Flow
workout.warmup: Start with two minutes of slow, natural breathing lying on your back. Let your shoulders drop, soften your jaw, and take five long exhales. Then roll slowly to one side and move into a seated position before beginning.

exercises.name: Seated Neck and Shoulder Release
exercises.notes: Sit cross-legged or in a chair. Drop one ear toward your shoulder, pause for three breaths, then slowly circle your chin toward your chest and to the other side. Keep it slow and deliberate. This is not a stretch competition.

exercises.name: Cat-Cow Spinal Flow
exercises.notes: On all fours, inhale to arch (cow), exhale to round (cat). Let your breath control the pace. If your wrists are sensitive, make fists or come down to forearms.

exercises.name: Thread-the-Needle Thoracic Rotation
exercises.notes: From all fours, slide one arm under your body along the floor, rotating your upper back. Follow your hand with your eyes. Hold the end position for two counts. Keep your hips stacked over your knees.

exercises.name: Low Lunge Hip Flexor Hold
exercises.notes: From a kneeling lunge, shift your hips forward gently until you feel a stretch at the front of the back hip. Keep your front knee stacked over your ankle. This is your desk-job antidote. Breathe into the tightness.

exercises.name: Supine Figure-Four Glute Stretch
exercises.notes: Lie on your back, cross one ankle over the opposite knee, and draw both legs toward your chest. Thread your hands around the back of the uncrossed thigh. If you feel it in the outer hip or glute, you are in the right place.

exercises.name: Legs-Up-the-Wall or Supported Bridge Hold
exercises.notes: Lie on your back and either rest your legs straight up a wall, or gently lift your hips into a passive bridge and hold softly. Focus on slow nasal breathing. This is your reset, not an exercise.

workout.cooldown: Finish flat on your back in a relaxed position for two to three minutes. Close your eyes, breathe naturally, and let your nervous system absorb the work. You can roll your feet out, turn your palms up, and do nothing at all.

Hold the end position for two counts. Keep your hips stacked over your knees. meal.title: Soft Polenta with Poached Eggs, Spinach & Roasted Cherry Tomatoes
meal.description: Creamy, slow-cooked polenta provides sustained carbohydrate energy for endurance training, while the poached eggs deliver choline for muscle coordination and two-day storage stability. Spinach and tomatoes round out the nutrient profile without adding heaviness.
ingredients: 2 cups fresh spinach (or 1 cup frozen, thawed)
Sea salt, black pepper, and red pepper flakes to taste
meal.instructions:
1. Toss cherry tomatoes with ½ tbsp olive oil, salt, and pepper. Spread on a sheet pan and roast at 400°F for 12–15 minutes until blistered and caramelized.
2. While tomatoes roast, bring milk and stock to a simmer in a medium saucepan over medium heat.
3. Slowly whisk in polenta cornmeal, stirring constantly to avoid lumps. Reduce heat to low and cook for 8–10 minutes, stirring frequently, until creamy and thick.
4. Stir in butter, Parmesan, salt, and pepper. Taste and adjust seasoning.
5. Heat ½ tbsp olive oil in a separate skillet over medium heat. Add garlic and fresh spinach, sautéing for 2 minutes until wilted. Season with salt and pepper.
6. To poach eggs: bring a pot of water to a gentle simmer, add vinegar. Create a gentle whirlpool and slide one egg into the center; cook 3 minutes for runny yolk. Repeat with second egg.
7. Divide polenta between bowls, top with wilted spinach and roasted tomatoes, and carefully place one poached egg on each. Garnish with red pepper flakes.
meal.tip: Make polenta ahead on Sunday—it keeps 4 days refrigerated and reheats beautifully with a splash of milk. Roast the tomatoes the night before, and simply wilt fresh spinach and poach eggs the morning of for a restaurant-quality 8-minute finish.
